title: Operational Shadows of Hilbert-Space Probabilities
abstract: At one frozen setting, the probabilities observed in a sharp quantum context are indistinguishable, as detector-click statistics, from ordinary probabilities on the atoms of a classical partition. But an actual analyzer usually comes with a calibrated knob: a tangible handle on the apparatus. If the measurement configuration is co-varied continuously through this physical parameter, the operational object is no longer one point of a simplex but a response curve. Classical linear responses, Malus-type Hilbert-space responses, softmax links, non-homomorphic parameter transcriptions, and discontinuous threshold limits are different maps from settings to probabilities. Continuity, calibration, and preservation of the physical composition law are then part of the experimental meaning of the knob. Such comparisons distinguish specified, calibrated response models; by themselves they do not constitute a classical-versus-quantum impossibility theorem. The static operational coincidence can also persist for two intertwined contexts: if the common outcomes receive the same probabilities, the remaining masses can always be coupled by a classical joint distribution. Genuine multi-context nonclassicality begins when a family of local shadows cannot be glued into one nonnegative global distribution or one simplex factorization. Farkas' lemma gives the exact alternative: either the classical extension exists, or a separating linear inequality certifies its impossibility.
summary: This theoretical work explores the operational meaning of measurement settings by analyzing probability 'response curves' generated when an apparatus parameter is varied continuously. It shows that while static measurements are insufficient to distinguish theories, genuine nonclassicality requires checking for global consistency across multiple contexts using tools like Farkas' lemma. The paper refines our understanding of contextuality beyond simple local inequalities.
main_problem: The paper aims to distinguish between different physical models (classical vs. quantum) by analyzing how probabilities change when a measurement apparatus setting is varied continuously.
main_result: While static measurements yield indistinguishable 'shadows' for classical and quantum theories, genuine nonclassicality emerges only when the family of local shadows cannot be consistently glued into one global distribution.
method: The analysis uses geometric constraints (like Farkas' lemma) applied to response functions derived from continuous variations of measurement settings ('knob sweeps').
model_or_system: The model involves a quantum system whose measurements are parameterized by a physical control variable, leading to a 'response curve' of probabilities on the simplex.
key_observables: Response curves $R_C: K 	o \Delta^{d-1}$, and the existence/non-existence of a global non-negative distribution for local shadows.
important_parameters: The continuous physical parameter controlling the measurement setting (the 'knob').
main_assumptions: It assumes that the experimental meaning of the knob requires continuity, calibration, and preservation of physical composition laws to distinguish models.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how different response laws (linear, quantum, softmax) must be read on different scales or through specific parameterizations to mimic each other, but this is not sufficient for a full Bell-type test.
paper_structure: The paper moves from analyzing static context shadows to dynamic response curves, then examines the limitations of pairwise correlations versus global consistency using linear feasibility systems and Farkas' lemma.
why_interesting: It provides a sophisticated mathematical framework for understanding how continuous experimental control over quantum measurements can reveal fundamental differences between classical probabilistic assumptions and true quantum mechanics, going beyond simple Bell tests.
